children.name: Deep Learning / LLM Foundations — universal-기초 concept dictionary

children.name: numerics-and-inference). This is the universal base…
children.detail: numerics-and-inference). This is the universal base layer that frontier-models.json (per-lab tricks) builds on; entries are general mechanisms, not vendor-specific. [reference primer for ARCHITECTURE.json ingestion; standard textbook concepts, timeless]

children.name: 역전파(backpropagation)
children.detail: 역전파(backpropagation): reverse-mode automatic differentiation applying the chain rule backward through the computation graph to compute every parameter's gradient in one pass — the engine of all neural-net training.

children.name: forward/backward pass
children.detail: forward/backward pass: forward computes outputs+loss layer-by-layer caching activations; backward propagates gradients from loss to inputs reusing those caches — one training step is forward then backward then update.

children.name: computational graph
children.detail: computational graph: a DAG of tensor ops (nodes) and data dependencies (edges) that autodiff traverses; static (compiled) or dynamic (define-by-run) graphs enable automatic gradient computation and op fusion.

children.name: 경사하강법(gradient descent / SGD)
children.detail: 경사하강법(gradient descent): iteratively step parameters opposite the loss gradient; SGD uses noisy mini-batch gradients, trading exactness for speed and an implicit regularizing noise that aids generalization.

children.name: momentum & Nesterov
children.detail: momentum: accumulate an exponentially-decayed velocity of past gradients to dampen oscillation and accelerate down ravines; Nesterov evaluates the gradient at the look-ahead point for a more responsive correction.

children.name: Adam / AdamW
children.detail: Adam: per-parameter adaptive LR from running 1st+2nd gradient moments; AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive step, fixing Adam's broken L2 and becoming the default LLM optimizer.

children.name: RMSprop / Adagrad
children.detail: RMSprop/Adagrad: scale each parameter's step by a running average of squared gradients so rare/large-gradient directions get smaller steps; Adagrad's sum monotonically shrinks LR, RMSprop's decay keeps it alive.

children.name: Adafactor
children.detail: Adafactor: memory-frugal Adam variant that factorizes the second-moment matrix into row/column statistics instead of storing it per-parameter, enabling large-model training under tight optimizer-state memory.

children.name: Muon
children.detail: Muon: a recent optimizer that orthogonalizes momentum updates for 2D weight matrices (via Newton–Schulz iteration), reported to improve token-efficiency on large LM pretraining versus AdamW.

children.name: learning-rate schedules
children.detail: LR schedules: vary step size over training — linear warmup ramps LR from ~0 to stabilize early unstable updates, then cosine/linear decay anneals toward 0 for a sharper final minimum.

children.name: loss functions
children.detail: loss functions: cross-entropy for classification/next-token (matches softmax, penalizes confident errors), MSE for regression, contrastive/InfoNCE pulls matched pairs together and pushes negatives apart.

children.name: vanishing/exploding gradients
children.detail: vanishing/exploding gradients: in deep/recurrent nets repeated Jacobian multiplication shrinks gradients to ~0 (no learning) or blows them up (instability); mitigated by residuals, normalization, init, and gating.

children.name: gradient clipping
children.detail: gradient clipping: cap the global gradient norm (or value) before the update so rare large gradients can't destabilize training — a cheap standard guard for exploding gradients in transformers and RNNs.

children.name: artificial neuron / MLP
children.detail: neuron/MLP: a neuron computes a weighted sum + bias through a nonlinearity; stacking fully-connected layers forms a multilayer perceptron, a universal function approximator and the transformer's FFN building block.

children.name: activation functions
children.detail: activations: nonlinearities that let nets model nonlinear maps — ReLU (cheap, sparse), GELU (smooth, transformer default), sigmoid/tanh (bounded, gate signals), SwiGLU (gated FFN boosting LLM quality).

children.name: softmax
children.detail: softmax: exponentiate-and-normalize a vector into a probability distribution; turns logits into class/token probabilities and forms attention weights, with temperature controlling sharpness.

children.name: 어텐션(scaled dot-product attention)
children.detail: 어텐션(attention): each query scores all keys via dot product scaled by 1/√d, softmaxes into weights, and returns a weighted sum of values — content-based routing that lets any token read from any other.

children.name: self vs cross attention
children.detail: self vs cross attention: self-attention has Q,K,V from the same sequence (modeling internal dependencies); cross-attention draws Q from one sequence and K,V from another (e.g. decoder attending to encoder).

children.name: multi-head attention (MHA)
children.detail: multi-head attention: run several attention heads in parallel on learned low-dim projections and concatenate, letting the model attend to different relationships/subspaces simultaneously.

children.name: MQA / GQA
children.detail: MQA/GQA: share K,V across heads to shrink the KV-cache — Multi-Query uses one K,V for all heads, Grouped-Query shares within head-groups, trading a little quality for big inference-memory/bandwidth savings.

children.name: KV-cache
children.detail: KV-cache: store past tokens' keys/values during autoregressive decoding so each new token attends without recomputing them — turns generation from O(n²) per step into O(n), at the cost of growing memory.

children.name: FlashAttention
children.detail: FlashAttention: IO-aware exact-attention kernel that tiles Q,K,V through fast SRAM and never materializes the full n×n score matrix, giving large speedups and linear memory in sequence length.

children.name: linear/sparse attention
children.detail: linear/sparse attention: approximate or restrict full attention to beat its O(n²) cost — sparse patterns (windowed/strided/global) or kernel linearizations trade some global reach for long-context scalability.

children.name: Transformer block & residual connections
children.detail: transformer block: stacked (attention + position-wise FFN) sublayers each wrapped with a residual skip connection so gradients flow and the block learns a refinement on top of identity.

children.name: LayerNorm vs RMSNorm
children.detail: LayerNorm vs RMSNorm: LayerNorm re-centers and re-scales activations per token (mean+variance); RMSNorm drops the mean step and normalizes by root-mean-square only — cheaper and now common in LLMs.

children.name: pre-norm vs post-norm
children.detail: pre-norm vs post-norm: post-norm (original) normalizes after the residual add; pre-norm normalizes inside the residual branch, giving much more stable gradients and enabling very deep transformer training.

children.name: FFN (feed-forward network)
children.detail: FFN: the per-token MLP in each transformer block (up-project → nonlinearity → down-project, typically 4×width); holds most parameters and acts as the model's key-value associative memory.

children.name: positional encoding
children.detail: positional encoding: inject token-order into permutation-invariant attention — fixed sinusoidal, learned embeddings, RoPE (rotate Q/K by position for relative encoding), or ALiBi (linear distance bias on scores).

children.name: embeddings & embedding matrix
children.detail: embeddings: a lookup matrix maps each token id to a dense vector the model operates on; tied embeddings reuse this matrix as the output projection, saving parameters and coupling input/output token spaces.

children.name: tokenization (BPE)
children.detail: tokenization: split text into subword units so a fixed vocabulary covers any string; Byte-Pair Encoding (and byte-level BPE) greedily merges frequent pairs, balancing vocab size against sequence length.

children.name: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)
children.detail: MoE: replace the FFN with many expert sub-networks plus a router that top-k-gates each token to a few experts, scaling total parameters while keeping per-token compute (active params) low.

children.name: MoE routing & load balancing
children.detail: MoE routing: the gating network picks experts per token; an auxiliary load-balancing loss (or aux-free bias) spreads tokens evenly so no expert is starved or overloaded and capacity isn't wasted.

children.name: convolution (CNN)
children.detail: convolution: slide shared learnable kernels over spatial input to extract translation-equivariant local features with weight sharing — the dominant vision primitive pre-transformers and still common in hybrids.

children.name: RNN / LSTM / GRU
children.detail: RNN/LSTM: process sequences step-by-step through a recurrent hidden state; LSTM/GRU add gates to carry long-range information past vanishing gradients — the pre-transformer sequence model, now mostly historical.

children.name: pretraining (causal/masked LM)
children.detail: pretraining: self-supervised learning on raw text — causal LM predicts the next token left-to-right (GPT-style), masked LM predicts held-out tokens from both sides (BERT-style); builds general representations cheaply.

children.name: fine-tuning (full)
children.detail: full fine-tuning: continue training all weights of a pretrained model on a downstream task/dataset — maximally expressive but costly in compute and storage and prone to overwriting general knowledge.

children.name: PEFT: LoRA / QLoRA / adapters
children.detail: PEFT: adapt a frozen model by training few extra params — LoRA injects low-rank ΔW matrices, QLoRA does LoRA over a 4-bit-quantized base, adapters insert small bottleneck layers; cheap, swappable, memory-light.

children.name: instruction tuning
children.detail: instruction tuning: supervised fine-tuning on (instruction, response) pairs so a base model follows natural-language commands and adopts a helpful assistant format — the SFT stage before preference alignment.

children.name: RLHF
children.detail: RLHF: align a model to human preferences — train a reward model from comparison data, then optimize the policy against it (often with PPO) under a KL penalty to stay near the reference model.

children.name: reward model
children.detail: reward model: a model trained on human (or AI) preference comparisons to score outputs, providing the scalar signal that RLHF/PPO optimizes — the learned proxy for 'what humans prefer'.

children.name: PPO
children.detail: PPO: the policy-gradient RL algorithm typical in RLHF; a clipped surrogate objective limits how far each update moves the policy, keeping training stable while maximizing the reward model's score.

children.name: DPO
children.detail: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization): skip the explicit reward model and RL loop by optimizing a closed-form classification loss directly on preference pairs — simpler and more stable than PPO-based RLHF.

children.name: GRPO
children.detail: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization): a critic-free RL method that estimates advantage from the mean reward of a sampled group of responses, cutting memory vs PPO; popular for reasoning/RLVR training.

children.name: KL penalty
children.detail: KL penalty: a divergence term keeping the trained policy close to the reference (SFT) model during RL, preventing reward-hacking and degeneration while still letting it improve on the reward signal.

children.name: knowledge distillation
children.detail: knowledge distillation: train a small STUDENT to mimic a large TEACHER's softened output distribution (temperature T>1 exposes 'dark knowledge' about inter-class similarity that a one-hot label discards) and/or its hidden states, via a loss mixing KL on the soft targets (scaled by T²) with cross-entropy on the hard labels; variants match the response/logits, intermediate features (FitNets), or sample-to-sample relations, and self/online (mutual) forms drop the fixed teacher; for generative LLMs the dominant practical form is sequence-level DATA distillation — the teacher generates completions/CoT that become an SFT dataset (cf. [[teacher-distillation-synthetic-data]]) — and it is orthogonal to, and routinely stacked with, quantization and pruning.

children.name: curriculum learning
children.detail: curriculum learning: order training data from easy to hard (or by quality/length) so the model builds foundations before difficult examples, often improving convergence speed and final quality.

children.name: data mixing
children.detail: data mixing: choose the proportions of corpora/domains (web, code, math, books) in the training mixture; weights strongly shape capabilities and are tuned, sometimes annealed, for the target skill profile.

children.name: catastrophic forgetting
children.detail: catastrophic forgetting: fine-tuning on new data erodes previously learned abilities as weights overwrite; countered by data replay, PEFT, regularization, or rehearsal to preserve old knowledge.

children.name: scaling laws (Chinchilla)
children.detail: scaling laws: loss falls as a smooth power law in params N, data D, and compute C; Chinchilla shows compute-optimal training scales D and N together (~20 tokens per parameter), favoring more data over sheer size.

children.name: mixed precision (FP16/BF16/FP8/FP4)
children.detail: mixed precision: compute in low precision (FP16/BF16, increasingly FP8/FP4) while keeping a master FP32 copy and loss-scaling, slashing memory+bandwidth and speeding tensor-core matmuls with little accuracy loss.

children.name: quantization (PTQ / QAT)
children.detail: quantization: represent weights/activations in low-bit ints/floats to shrink and accelerate models — PTQ calibrates an already-trained model, quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates it during training for accuracy.

children.name: GPTQ / AWQ
children.detail: GPTQ/AWQ: weight-only PTQ for LLMs — GPTQ minimizes per-layer reconstruction error via second-order updates, AWQ scales activation-salient weights before rounding; both give ~4-bit inference with minimal quality drop.

children.name: GGUF k-quants
children.detail: GGUF k-quants: the llama.cpp file format and block-wise mixed-bit quantization schemes (Q4_K, Q5_K, …) that allocate more bits to sensitive weights, enabling efficient CPU/consumer-GPU local inference.

children.name: sampling/decoding
children.detail: decoding: choose the next token from the output distribution — greedy/argmax (deterministic), temperature (rescale randomness), top-k (k likeliest), top-p/nucleus (smallest mass-p set), balancing quality vs diversity.

children.name: beam search
children.detail: beam search: keep the top-B partial sequences by cumulative log-prob at each step, exploring multiple hypotheses for higher-likelihood outputs; strong for translation but tends to bland text in open-ended generation.

children.name: speculative decoding
children.detail: speculative decoding: a cheap draft model proposes several tokens that the big model verifies in one parallel pass, accepting the matching prefix — lossless speedup that exploits spare compute to cut latency.

children.name: continuous batching
children.detail: continuous/in-flight batching: serving scheduler that adds and evicts requests at the token level instead of waiting for a whole batch, keeping the GPU saturated and maximizing throughput under mixed-length traffic.

children.name: bias-variance tradeoff
children.detail: bias-variance tradeoff: error decomposes into bias (underfitting, too-simple model) and variance (overfitting, too data-sensitive); generalization comes from balancing the two via capacity and regularization.

children.name: regularization
children.detail: regularization: techniques to curb overfitting — dropout randomly zeros activations, weight decay penalizes large weights, label smoothing softens targets, early stopping halts at best validation loss.

children.name: title
children.detail: Reasoning methods

children.name: chain-of-thought
children.detail: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits intermediate natural-language reasoning steps before the final answer, raising accuracy on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic tasks versus direct answering.

children.name: zero-shot-cot
children.detail: Zero-shot CoT triggers step-by-step reasoning without exemplars by appending a cue such as 'Let's think step by step', recovering much of few-shot CoT's gain with no hand-written demonstrations.

children.name: self-consistency
children.detail: Self-consistency samples multiple CoT reasoning paths at temperature>0 and marginalizes by majority vote over final answers, trading extra inference compute for substantially higher accuracy than greedy decoding.

children.name: tree-of-thoughts
children.detail: Tree-of-thoughts (ToT) frames reasoning as search over a tree of intermediate thought states with explicit branching, value-based evaluation, and backtracking (BFS/DFS), beating linear CoT on planning/search tasks.

children.name: least-to-most
children.detail: Least-to-most prompting decomposes a hard problem into an ordered chain of easier subproblems, solving each and feeding its answer forward, enabling compositional and length generalization beyond CoT.

children.name: scratchpad
children.detail: Scratchpad prompting lets the model emit intermediate working (carries, partial states, program traces) into a buffer before answering, improving multi-step algorithmic and arithmetic execution.

children.name: reasoning-models
children.detail: Reasoning models (o1-style / long-thinking) are RL-trained to produce extended internal chains of thought before answering, scaling reliability on math, coding, and science by deliberating longer at inference.

children.name: test-time-compute-scaling
children.detail: Test-time (inference-time) compute scaling spends more tokens/samples per query — longer CoT, parallel sampling, search, verification — to lift accuracy, an axis distinct from and tradeable against pretraining scale.

children.name: verifier-prm
children.detail: Verifiers and process reward models (PRM) score reasoning per-step or per-solution; PRMs reward each correct intermediate step (vs outcome-only ORMs), guiding search/best-of-N selection and RL on reasoning traces.

children.name: title
children.detail: Agent patterns & orchestration

children.name: react
children.detail: ReAct interleaves reasoning traces (Thought) with actions (tool/API calls) and observations in a loop, letting the model plan, act in an environment, and incorporate results to reduce hallucination.

children.name: reflexion
children.detail: Reflexion adds verbal self-reflection: after a failed attempt the agent writes a critique to episodic memory and retries, learning across trials via language feedback rather than weight updates.

children.name: plan-and-execute
children.detail: Plan-and-execute agents first draft a multi-step plan with a planner, then dispatch each step to an executor (often per-step tool calls), separating high-level strategy from step execution for long tasks.

children.name: tool-use-function-calling
children.detail: Tool use / function calling lets an LLM emit a structured call (name + JSON arguments) against a declared schema; the runtime executes it and returns results, grounding the model in external systems and data.

children.name: mcp-tool-protocols
children.detail: MCP (Model Context Protocol) and similar tool protocols standardize how agents discover and invoke external tools, resources, and prompts over a client-server interface, decoupling models from bespoke integrations.

children.name: code-as-action
children.detail: Code-as-action agents emit executable code (e.g. Python) as their action space instead of fixed JSON tool calls, gaining composability, control flow, and reuse — the model orchestrates via a sandboxed interpreter.

children.name: multi-agent-orchestration
children.detail: Multi-agent orchestration coordinates specialized agents (planner, researcher, critic, executor) via a supervisor/handoff or debate topology, parallelizing subtasks and cross-checking at coordination cost.

children.name: router-vs-in-weight-routing
children.detail: Routing sends a query to a model/tool/expert: in-weight routing learns the choice in parameters (e.g. MoE gating) vs an external router over models — hexa-codex routes out-of-weights via atlas retrieval, not parameters.

children.name: title
children.detail: Memory & retrieval

children.name: context-window
children.detail: The context window is the bounded token span an LLM attends over per call; everything an agent 'knows' in the moment must fit it, making context budgeting, compaction, and selection core agent concerns.

children.name: rag
children.detail: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fetches relevant external documents at query time and prepends them to the prompt, grounding answers in up-to-date or private knowledge without retraining and curbing hallucination.

children.name: vector-db-embeddings
children.detail: Vector databases index dense embeddings of chunks and serve approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) similarity search, the standard retrieval backend for RAG and semantic memory, often hybridized with keyword/BM25.

children.name: long-context
children.detail: Long-context methods (positional interpolation/RoPE scaling, sparse/flash attention, ring attention) extend usable context to hundreds of thousands of tokens, though attention cost and lost-in-the-middle effects persist.

children.name: kv-cache-reuse
children.detail: KV-cache reuse stores attention key/value tensors for already-processed tokens so shared prefixes (system prompts, retrieved docs) are not recomputed, via prefix caching that cuts latency and repeat-prompt cost.

children.name: memory-persistence
children.detail: Memory/scratchpad persistence externalizes state across turns or sessions — episodic notes, summaries, key-value stores, or files — letting agents accumulate facts and reflections beyond a single context window.

children.name: title
children.detail: RL environments & execution

children.name: verifiable-reward-rl
children.detail: Verifiable-reward RL (RLVR) trains on tasks with programmatic ground-truth checks — unit tests, exact-match, theorem provers — yielding clean, unhackable reward signals that drive reasoning-model and agent gains.

children.name: sandboxed-execution
children.detail: Sandboxed execution runs agent-generated code or tool actions in an isolated container/VM with resource and network limits, enabling safe code-as-action, real test feedback, and reproducible environment rollouts.

children.name: tool-synthesis
children.detail: Tool synthesis has agents author, register, and reuse their own tools/functions on demand — generating helper code that becomes a callable, growing an environment's action space rather than relying only on fixed APIs.

children.name: title
children.detail: Prompting techniques

children.name: few-shot
children.detail: Few-shot (in-context) prompting supplies a handful of input-output exemplars in the prompt so the model infers the task at inference time with no weight updates — exemplar choice/order materially affects results.

children.name: system-prompt
children.detail: The system prompt sets the agent's persistent role, constraints, tools, and policies above the user turn, steering behavior and safety; it is the highest-leverage, most cache-friendly slice of the context.

children.name: structured-output-json-mode
children.detail: Structured output / JSON mode constrains generation to a schema (JSON Schema, grammar-constrained decoding) so responses parse reliably into typed fields, essential for tool calls and downstream pipelines.

children.name: prompt-engineering
children.detail: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing instructions, exemplars, formatting, decomposition, and delimiters to shape LLM behavior reliably — increasingly augmented by automatic prompt optimization and evaluation.

children.name: vision-encoders
children.detail: Models mapping pixels to feature vectors — the perception front-end of vision and vision-language systems.

children.name: cnn-recap
children.detail: Convolutional nets (AlexNet/VGG/ResNet) build a spatial feature hierarchy via learned local kernels with weight-sharing, pooling, and residual skips, giving translation-equivariance and strong small-data bias.

children.name: vit-patch-embedding
children.detail: Vision Transformer cuts an image into fixed patches (e.g. 16x16), linearly projects each into a token, adds positional embeddings plus a [CLS] token, then runs a plain transformer — trading CNN bias for scale.

children.name: clip-contrastive
children.detail: CLIP co-trains image and text encoders with an InfoNCE contrastive loss pulling matched image-caption pairs together and mismatches apart in a shared space, enabling zero-shot open-vocabulary transfer from web pairs.

children.name: siglip
children.detail: SigLIP swaps CLIP's softmax-over-batch loss for a pairwise sigmoid loss per image-text pair, decoupling from giant batch sizes, improving small-batch efficiency, and yielding stronger frozen features for VLM backbones.

children.name: vlm-fusion
children.detail: How vision features are injected into a language model to form a vision-language model (VLM).

children.name: cross-attention-vs-early-fusion
children.detail: Cross-attention fusion (Flamingo) keeps the LLM frozen and inserts gated cross-attention to vision features, while early-fusion/token-merge concatenates projected image tokens so one self-attention mixes both.

children.name: projector-connector
children.detail: The projector (connector/adapter) bridges frozen vision-encoder embeddings into LLM token space and dimensionality — a linear layer, MLP, Q-Former, or perceiver-resampler — often the only module trained in stage-1.

children.name: llava-style
children.detail: LLaVA wires a frozen CLIP/SigLIP encoder to an LLM via a light MLP projector, trained on GPT-generated visual-instruction data in two stages (projector pretrain then end-to-end tune) — the dominant open VLM recipe.

children.name: native-multimodal
children.detail: Natively-multimodal models (GPT-4o, Gemini, Chameleon) pretrain from scratch on interleaved text-image(-audio) tokens in one transformer rather than bolting a vision adapter onto a text LLM, enabling tighter grounding.

children.name: any-resolution-tiling
children.detail: AnyRes / dynamic high-res tiling (LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen2-VL, InternVL) splits a large image into a grid of separately-encoded sub-tiles plus a global thumbnail, raising resolution for OCR and dense scenes at more tokens.

children.name: image-generation
children.detail: Likelihood and sampling families for synthesizing images from noise or conditions.

children.name: gan
children.detail: Generative Adversarial Networks train a generator against a discriminator in a minimax game so samples become indistinguishable from real, giving sharp single-step synthesis (StyleGAN) but mode collapse and instability.

children.name: vae
children.detail: Variational Autoencoders encode inputs to a regularized latent distribution and decode samples, maximizing the ELBO (reconstruction + KL-to-prior); they give a structured continuous latent and stable training, but blur.

children.name: ddpm
children.detail: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models add Gaussian noise over T forward steps and train a net to predict that noise (epsilon-prediction) for the reverse denoising chain, yielding high-fidelity samples over many steps.

children.name: ddim
children.detail: DDIM recasts the diffusion reverse process as a deterministic non-Markovian ODE trajectory, enabling far fewer sampling steps and reproducible, interpolatable generations from a noise seed without retraining.

children.name: latent-diffusion-stable-diffusion
children.detail: Latent Diffusion (Stable Diffusion) runs diffusion in a VAE-compressed latent not pixel space, slashing compute, with a U-Net/DiT denoiser conditioned on text via cross-attention — the canonical text-to-image stack.

children.name: classifier-free-guidance
children.detail: Classifier-free guidance trains conditional and unconditional denoisers jointly (random condition dropout) and at sampling extrapolates from the unconditional prediction by a guidance scale, trading diversity for fit.

children.name: flow-matching
children.detail: Flow matching trains a continuous-time vector field by regressing a conditional probability-path velocity (simulation-free), generalizing diffusion as a continuous normalizing flow and underpinning SD3 and Flux.

children.name: rectified-flow
children.detail: Rectified flow learns straight transport paths between noise and data by linear interpolation plus optional reflow, straightening trajectories so samples need very few (even one) ODE steps — fast SD3/Flux sampling.

children.name: autoregressive-image
children.detail: Treating images as discrete token sequences for transformer next-token generation.

children.name: vq-vae
children.detail: VQ-VAE encodes an image to a grid of discrete codes by nearest-neighbor lookup into a learned codebook (straight-through gradient + commitment loss), turning pixels into a compact token map an AR prior can model.

children.name: vqgan-tokenized-image
children.detail: VQGAN adds adversarial and perceptual losses to VQ-VAE for sharper high-res reconstructions; its image tokens feed transformer priors (DALL-E 1, Parti, MaskGIT) so image synthesis becomes sequence modeling.

children.name: audio-speech
children.detail: Speech recognition, neural audio compression, and speech synthesis.

children.name: whisper-asr
children.detail: Whisper is an encoder-decoder transformer trained on ~680k hours of weakly-supervised multilingual audio for robust ASR, translation, and language ID over log-Mel spectrograms with task tokens and zero-shot robustness.

children.name: neural-audio-codec
children.detail: Neural codecs (SoundStream, EnCodec, DAC) use a convolutional VQ-VAE with residual vector quantization to compress waveforms into stacked discrete audio tokens, the vocabulary audio LMs (AudioLM, MusicGen, VALL-E) model.

children.name: tts
children.detail: Text-to-speech moved from concatenative to neural acoustic models (Tacotron, FastSpeech) plus vocoders (WaveNet, HiFi-GAN), and now token-based zero-shot voice cloning (VALL-E) and diffusion/flow with natural prosody.

children.name: video-3d
children.detail: Temporal video generation and 3D scene representation (brief coverage).

children.name: video-generation
children.detail: Video models extend latent diffusion with spatiotemporal (often factorized space-time) attention over a learned video VAE; Sora and Veo generate temporally-coherent clips from text on long-context DiT backbones.

children.name: nerf-3d
children.detail: Neural Radiance Fields encode a scene as an MLP from 3D position and view direction to color and density, rendered via differentiable volume ray-marching from posed images; 3D Gaussian Splatting later replaced it.

children.name: document-perception
children.detail: Reading text in images, structured document understanding, and perception-counting limits relevant to hexa-codex's SANDBOX subitizing lane.

children.name: ocr
children.detail: Optical Character Recognition localizes and transcribes image text; classical pipelines (detection + CRNN/CTC, Tesseract) gave way to transformer OCR (TrOCR) and general VLMs reading text end-to-end without an OCR stage.

children.name: document-understanding
children.detail: Document AI (LayoutLM, Donut, Pix2Struct) jointly models text, 2D layout coordinates, and image features to answer over forms, tables, charts, and receipts; OCR-free models read page pixels into structured output.

children.name: subitizing-counting-limit
children.detail: Subitizing is instant accurate enumeration of ~1-4 items; VLMs show an analogous ceiling where counting 5-9 dense objects breaks the monotone capability-vs-scale trend (hexa-codex SANDBOX: Qwen2.5-VL-3B drops to 2/5).

children.name: omni-models
children.detail: Unified any-to-any models spanning many modalities in one network.

children.name: any-to-any-omni
children.detail: Any-to-any / omni models (GPT-4o, Gemini, AnyGPT, Unified-IO) accept and emit arbitrary combinations of text, image, audio, and video through a shared token space and one transformer for unified understand-and-generate.

children.name: training-systems
children.detail: Parallelism, memory, kernel, serving, queueing, and hardware substrate behind large-model training and inference.

children.name: title
children.detail: Training systems & infrastructure

children.name: data-parallelism
children.detail: Data parallelism replicates the whole model per device, splits the global batch across them, and averages gradients by all-reduce each step; near-linear throughput but capped by per-device memory holding the full model.

children.name: model-parallelism
children.detail: Model (inter-op) parallelism partitions a model's layers across devices so one model spans many GPUs, lifting the single-device memory cap at the cost of cross-device activation transfer and pipeline-bubble idle time.

children.name: tensor-parallelism
children.detail: Tensor (intra-op) parallelism shards weight matrices row/column-wise across devices, computing matmuls in parallel and stitching via all-reduce/all-gather; communication-heavy, so kept within a fast NVLink island.

children.name: pipeline-parallelism
children.detail: Pipeline parallelism maps contiguous layer stages to devices and streams micro-batches through them (GPipe/1F1B), trading a startup/drain bubble to train models larger than one device while keeping stages busy.

children.name: sequence-parallelism
children.detail: Sequence/context parallelism splits the token dimension across devices (sharded LayerNorm/dropout, Ring/Ulysses attention), cutting activation memory for very long contexts that tensor parallelism alone cannot fit.

children.name: zero-fsdp-deepspeed
children.detail: ZeRO (DeepSpeed) and PyTorch FSDP shard optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across data-parallel ranks (ZeRO 1/2/3), gathering each shard per layer for model-parallel savings with a data-parallel API.

children.name: megatron-lm
children.detail: Megatron-LM is NVIDIA's reference framework composing tensor + pipeline + data parallelism (3D, often with ZeRO) plus fused kernels to train transformer LLMs efficiently across thousands of GPUs.

children.name: gradient-accumulation
children.detail: Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several forward/backward micro-batches before one optimizer step, emulating a large effective batch on limited memory at the cost of more steps per weight update.

children.name: activation-checkpointing
children.detail: Activation (gradient) checkpointing discards intermediate activations in the forward pass and recomputes them in backward, trading roughly one extra forward of compute for a large cut in peak activation memory.

children.name: mixed-precision-training
children.detail: Mixed-precision training runs matmuls in 16-bit (FP16/BF16, now FP8) while keeping FP32 master weights and (for FP16) loss scaling, roughly halving memory/bandwidth and using tensor cores with little accuracy loss.

children.name: collective-all-reduce
children.detail: Distributed training relies on collectives (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast) via NCCL with ring/tree algorithms over NVLink/InfiniBand; gradient all-reduce dominates synchronous data-parallel traffic.

children.name: accelerators-hbm-memory-wall
children.detail: GPUs/TPUs and other accelerators pair many parallel ALUs with high-bandwidth memory (HBM); since FLOPs grow faster than bandwidth, large-model speed is increasingly bound by the memory wall, not raw arithmetic.

children.name: kernel-fusion-flashattention
children.detail: Kernel fusion merges ops into one GPU kernel to cut HBM round-trips; FlashAttention is the canonical case, an IO-aware tiled kernel that never materializes the full score matrix, making attention memory-linear.

children.name: vllm-pagedattention
children.detail: vLLM serves LLMs with PagedAttention, storing the KV cache in non-contiguous fixed-size blocks (OS-style paging) to nearly eliminate fragmentation, enabling high-throughput continuous batching and KV sharing.

children.name: batching-throughput-vs-latency
children.detail: Inference trades throughput against latency: bigger/continuous batches amortize weight loads but add queueing delay, so capacity is sized via queueing theory (M/M/c, Erlang-C) for a tail-latency SLO (hexa-codex OPS).

children.name: roofline-model
children.detail: The roofline model plots attainable FLOP/s vs arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte): low-intensity kernels are bandwidth-bound and high-intensity ones compute-bound, diagnosing whether to fuse/recompute or add FLOPs.

children.name: training-cost-economics
children.detail: Training cost is GPU-hours × price, driven by total FLOPs (~6·N·D for N params over D tokens), achieved utilization (MFU), interconnect efficiency, and restart overhead; frontier runs reach tens of millions of dollars.

children.name: domestic-silicon-ascend
children.detail: Sovereign/domestic accelerators (Huawei Ascend with CANN, Google TPU, AWS Trainium/Inferentia) pursue non-NVIDIA capacity, trading a less mature software stack for supply-chain and export-control independence.

children.name: history-lineage
children.detail: Dated lineage of the ideas and models leading to modern LLMs, from the 1958 perceptron to the reasoning-model and MoE-at-scale eras.

children.name: title
children.detail: AI history & lineage

children.name: perceptron-1958
children.detail: In 1958 Frank Rosenblatt introduced the perceptron, a trainable single-layer linear threshold classifier; its inability to learn XOR (Minsky & Papert, 1969) helped trigger the first AI winter.

children.name: backprop-1986
children.detail: Backpropagation, efficient chain-rule gradient computation through layers, was popularized for neural nets by Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams in 1986, making multi-layer deep networks trainable.

children.name: cnn-lenet-alexnet-1989-2012
children.detail: Convolutional nets matured from LeCun's backprop-trained digit recognizer (LeNet, ~1989/1998) to AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, 2012), whose GPU ImageNet win launched the deep-learning boom.

children.name: word2vec-embeddings-2013
children.detail: In 2013 Mikolov et al. released word2vec (skip-gram/CBOW), learning dense distributed word embeddings whose vector geometry captures semantic and analogical relations, establishing learned representations in NLP.

children.name: seq2seq-attention-2014
children.detail: In 2014 Sutskever et al. introduced sequence-to-sequence encoder-decoder RNNs, and Bahdanau et al. added attention letting the decoder soft-align to encoder states, fixing the fixed-vector bottleneck in translation.

children.name: transformer-2017
children.detail: The 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al.) introduced the Transformer, replacing recurrence with stacked self-attention and feed-forward blocks; its parallelizable architecture became the LLM backbone.

children.name: bert-gpt-2018
children.detail: In 2018 two transformer pretraining paradigms emerged: OpenAI's GPT (autoregressive decoder, generative) and Google's BERT (bidirectional masked-LM encoder), establishing self-supervised pretrain-then-finetune.

children.name: scaling-laws-gpt3-2020
children.detail: In 2020 Kaplan et al. published neural scaling laws (loss as a power law in params, data, compute) and OpenAI's 175B-parameter GPT-3 showed strong few-shot in-context learning, validating scale as a primary lever.

children.name: instructgpt-rlhf-2022
children.detail: In 2022 OpenAI's InstructGPT showed reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) — instruction tuning plus a learned reward model optimized with PPO — aligns outputs to human intent far better than scale alone.

children.name: chatgpt-moment-2022
children.detail: ChatGPT, released November 2022, packaged an RLHF-tuned GPT-3.5 as a free conversational interface and reached ~100M users within two months, igniting mainstream awareness and the generative-AI race.

children.name: open-weight-era-2023
children.detail: From Meta's LLaMA (Feb 2023) and openly licensed Llama 2 (July 2023), alongside Mistral, Falcon, and later Qwen/DeepSeek, downloadable open-weight models enabled local finetuning and a fast community ecosystem.

children.name: reasoning-model-era-2024
children.detail: From late 2024 the reasoning-model era began with OpenAI's o1 (then o3, DeepSeek-R1), spending extra inference-time compute on long RL-trained chain-of-thought, sharply improving math, coding, and multi-step reasoning.

children.name: moe-at-scale-era
children.detail: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) scaling, popularized by GShard/Switch Transformer and reaching the frontier with Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3, routes each token to a few of many expert FFNs: huge params, low active cost.

children.name: benchmark-families
children.detail: Standardized datasets/leaderboards that probe a capability axis (knowledge, math, code, reasoning, instruction-following, dialogue, agentic) and emit a comparable score.

children.name: MMLU / MMLU-Pro
children.detail: Massive Multitask Language Understanding: 4-choice exam over 57 academic subjects; near-saturated (>90%), so MMLU-Pro hardened it to 10 choices, reasoning-heavy questions, and reduced answer-pattern leakage.

children.name: GPQA
children.detail: Graduate-level Google-Proof Q&A: ~448 PhD-written biology/chemistry/physics MCQs, expert-validated to resist web lookup; the 'Diamond' subset is the hard-difficulty standard for frontier reasoning models.

children.name: GSM8K / MATH
children.detail: GSM8K = ~8.5k grade-school multi-step arithmetic word problems (now largely saturated); MATH = 12.5k competition problems across 5 difficulty levels, the canonical harder math benchmark before AIME-class evals.

children.name: HumanEval / MBPP
children.detail: Function-synthesis code benchmarks: HumanEval = 164 hand-written Python problems scored by hidden unit tests via pass@k; MBPP = ~1k entry-level tasks. Both small, saturated, and contamination-prone.

children.name: SWE-bench
children.detail: Real GitHub issues where the model must produce a patch passing the repo's tests; SWE-bench Verified (~500 human-validated tasks) is the agentic software-engineering standard, far harder than HumanEval.

children.name: BIG-Bench / BBH
children.detail: BIG-Bench = 200+ collaboratively-authored diverse tasks; BBH (BIG-Bench Hard) = the 23 tasks where models then trailed humans, and the benchmark that popularized chain-of-thought lifting accuracy sharply.

children.name: HellaSwag / ARC / Winogrande
children.detail: Classic commonsense MCQ suites (sentence completion, science exam, Winograd coreference) once core to leaderboards; now saturated by frontier models, mainly used for small-model and pretraining-quality comparison.

children.name: IFEval
children.detail: Instruction-Following Eval: prompts with verifiable constraints (word count, JSON format, forbidden words, casing) checked by deterministic code, giving a judge-free objective measure of literal instruction adherence.

children.name: MT-Bench
children.detail: 80 multi-turn open-ended prompts across 8 categories scored 1-10 by an LLM judge (typically GPT-4); an early, cheap, automated proxy for chat quality, now superseded by larger arena-style evals.

children.name: Chatbot Arena / Elo
children.detail: Crowdsourced blind pairwise human votes between two anonymous models on real prompts, aggregated into Bradley-Terry/Elo ratings; the de-facto human-preference leaderboard, though style/length-biased and gameable.

children.name: LiveBench
children.detail: Contamination-resistant benchmark that continuously refreshes questions from recent sources (news, papers, competitions) with objective ground-truth answers, designed so models cannot have trained on the test items.

children.name: AIME
children.detail: American Invitational Mathematics Examination: 15 integer-answer competition problems per year; a hard exact-match math benchmark used to differentiate reasoning models, but tiny (high variance) and freshness-sensitive.

children.name: tau-bench (τ-bench)
children.detail: Agentic tool-use benchmark simulating customer-service workflows (retail/airline): the model follows domain policy, calls tools, and converses with a simulated user; scored by end-state correctness + pass^k consistency.

children.name: GAIA
children.detail: General AI Assistants benchmark: 466 real-world questions needing multi-step web browsing, tool use, and multimodal reasoning with unambiguous answers; easy for humans (~92%) but hard for assistants.

children.name: metrics
children.detail: Scalar functions that reduce model outputs to a comparable number — correctness, fluency-overlap, preference, and calibration measures.

children.name: pass@k
children.detail: Probability that at least one of k sampled generations passes the (usually test-based) checker; an unbiased estimator from n>=k samples rewarding coverage under sampling (pass@1 = single-shot correctness).

children.name: exact-match / accuracy
children.detail: Binary scoring of whether the normalized output equals the gold answer; reproducible for MCQ/integer tasks but brittle to formatting, needing answer-extraction (e.g. \boxed{} parsing) so correct outputs aren't failed.

children.name: perplexity
children.detail: exp of the mean per-token negative log-likelihood on held-out text; an intrinsic LM metric (lower = better next-token prediction) for pretraining quality, but tokenizer-dependent and weakly correlated with task ability.

children.name: BLEU / ROUGE
children.detail: N-gram-overlap metrics for translation (BLEU, precision + brevity penalty) and summarization (ROUGE, recall-oriented); cheap and reproducible but reward surface lexical match, missing paraphrase and valid alternatives.

children.name: win-rate
children.detail: Fraction of pairwise comparisons a model wins against a baseline (human or LLM judge), often length/position-controlled (e.g. AlpacaEval LC); the core aggregate behind preference leaderboards, prone to verbosity bias.

children.name: calibration: Brier / ECE
children.detail: Whether stated confidence matches empirical accuracy: Brier = mean squared error of probabilistic predictions; ECE (Expected Calibration Error) = binned accuracy-vs-confidence gap. RLHF often hurts it (overconfidence).

children.name: methodology
children.detail: Evaluation protocol choices — how prompts are constructed, how reasoning is elicited, how outputs are judged, and how test-time compute is scaled — that materially move scores at fixed model weights.

children.name: zero-shot vs few-shot
children.detail: Whether the prompt includes in-context worked examples (k-shot) before the test item; few-shot fixes output format and lifts weaker models, but shot count and exemplar choice are a tunable knob that confounds comparison.

children.name: chain-of-thought (CoT) effect
children.detail: Prompting step-by-step reasoning before the answer; raises accuracy on multi-step math/logic (the BBH lift) but inflates tokens, so the benchmark measures reasoning-with-scaffolding, not single-pass ability.

children.name: contamination / leakage
children.detail: Test items (or near-duplicates) in pretraining data inflate scores without real capability; detected via n-gram overlap, canary strings, and memorization probes — the central threat to any static public benchmark.

children.name: LLM-as-judge & its biases
children.detail: Scoring outputs with a strong model scales cheaply but injects biases: position bias (first/second), verbosity bias, self-enhancement (favoring its own family), and sycophancy; mitigated by order-swapping.

children.name: self-consistency
children.detail: Sample multiple CoT reasoning paths and take the majority-vote answer; trades extra inference compute for accuracy on discrete-answer tasks — a standard test-time-compute method, distinct from but related to pass@k.

children.name: test-time scaling eval
children.detail: Measuring accuracy as a function of inference compute (samples, reasoning-token budget, best-of-n search) rather than a single point; needed to compare reasoning models fairly since score depends on thinking budget.

children.name: reliability
children.detail: Properties governing whether a benchmark number is stable, meaningful, and still discriminative — variance, sensitivity, headroom, and the proxy-vs-target failure mode.

children.name: variance / statistical significance
children.detail: Small benchmarks (AIME 15q, GPQA Diamond ~198q) and stochastic sampling give wide confidence intervals, so leaderboard gaps of a few points are often noise; honest reporting needs multiple seeds and CIs.

children.name: prompt sensitivity
children.detail: Scores swing several points from cosmetic changes — option ordering, MCQ labels, system-prompt wording, whitespace, answer-extraction regex — so a number reflects the harness's prompt template as much as the model.

children.name: saturation
children.detail: When top models cluster near the ceiling (MMLU/GSM8K/HellaSwag >90%), the benchmark loses discriminative power and gaps are dominated by label noise, forcing migration to harder successors (MMLU-Pro, GPQA, FrontierMath).

children.name: Goodhart's law on benchmarks
children.detail: When a benchmark becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure: optimizing directly toward leaderboard scores decouples them from real capability, so a headline metric decays as a proxy as the field competes on it.

children.name: pitfalls
children.detail: Concrete ways reported scores mislead — deliberate gaming, train-on-test leakage, and format artifacts — that an evaluator must actively defend against.

children.name: benchmark gaming
children.detail: Tailoring a model to known eval distributions — style/verbosity tuning for Arena, format-matching the judge, picking best-of-many checkpoints on the test set — lifting the number without real capability gain.

children.name: train-on-test
children.detail: Including benchmark test splits (or their solutions) in training data, accidental or deliberate; the most direct score inflation, defended by held-out sets, canaries, and fresh questions (LiveBench).

children.name: format bias
children.detail: Scores distorted by output-format mismatch not reasoning: exact-match failing differently-wrapped answers, MCQ first-token-logit vs free-generation disagreeing, parse failures counted wrong — a harness artifact.

children.name: alignment-problem
children.detail: Making AI pursue the operator's intended goals and human values rather than a literal proxy; splits into outer alignment (specifying the right objective) and inner alignment (the trained model actually adopting it).

children.name: specification-gaming
children.detail: Maximizing the literal specified objective via unintended loopholes that violate intent (exploiting a simulator bug, pausing a game to avoid losing); a symptom of misspecified reward, not capability failure.

children.name: reward-hacking
children.detail: The RLHF case where a policy exploits flaws in a learned reward model to score high without desired behavior; verbosity/format bias, reward-model over-optimization (Goodhart), and KL-budget exploitation are canonical.

children.name: goodharts-law
children.detail: "When a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure" — behind reward-model over-optimization: pushing too far against an imperfect proxy eventually lowers true reward, motivating KL regularization.

children.name: instrumental-convergence-and-power-seeking
children.detail: The argument that for a broad range of final goals a capable agent acquires convergent subgoals — self-preservation, resource acquisition, goal-integrity, resisting shutdown — motivating corrigibility research.

children.name: rlhf-alignment-vs-capability
children.detail: RLHF mainly aligns behavior (eliciting helpful, harmless, honest answers and refusals) not capability; its risk is teaching the surface form judges reward, enabling sycophancy and reward hacking over intent.

children.name: constitutional-ai
children.detail: Anthropic's method replacing human harm-feedback with a written constitution: the model critiques and revises its outputs against principles, then RLAIF trains on AI-generated preference labels, cutting labeler exposure.

children.name: rlaif
children.detail: RL from AI Feedback: an LLM generates the preference labels or rewards used for alignment, scaling oversight past human throughput; safety hinges on the labeler's own alignment, risking propagation of its blind spots.

children.name: dpo-as-alignment
children.detail: Direct Preference Optimization reframes RLHF as one classification loss on preferred/dispreferred pairs with an implicit reward, dropping the reward model and PPO loop; stabler but over-fits and inherits length bias.

children.name: ipo-kto-and-preference-variants
children.detail: DPO successors fixing its failure modes: IPO regularizes over-confident preferences, KTO learns from cheap binary good/bad signals via a prospect-theory loss, ORPO/SimPO fold preference into SFT without a reference.

children.name: refusal-and-safety-training
children.detail: Targeted alignment to decline harmful/out-of-policy requests while staying helpful on benign ones; over-refusal and paraphrase-inconsistency are failure modes, and refusal can be a shallow direction fine-tuning strips.

children.name: scalable-oversight
children.detail: Techniques to supervise models on tasks humans cannot directly check (superhuman or costly-to-verify outputs), amplifying a weak overseer's judgment so the training signal stays trustworthy as capability outpaces humans.

children.name: debate
children.detail: A scalable-oversight protocol where two models argue opposing answers and a weaker judge decides, betting exposing flaws is easier than producing them so truth wins; vulnerable to obfuscated, persuasive-wrong arguments.

children.name: recursive-reward-modeling
children.detail: Iterated amplification: models assist humans in evaluating outputs, and those assisted judgments train reward models for harder tasks, bootstrapping oversight up a capability ladder while each rung stays human-checkable.

children.name: weak-to-strong-generalization
children.detail: OpenAI's setup where a weak supervisor's labels elicit a strong model's latent capability; the student often generalizes beyond its teacher's errors — a toy analogy for aligning superhuman models, recovery only partial.

children.name: mechanistic-interpretability
children.detail: Reverse-engineering networks into human-understandable algorithms — features, circuits, computations in weights/activations — to audit, predict, and edit behavior; the backbone for catching hidden misalignment.

children.name: sparse-autoencoders-and-features
children.detail: SAEs decompose superposed polysemantic activations into a large sparse dictionary of monosemantic features, tackling superposition so interpretable concepts can be read out, monitored, and clamped for steering.

children.name: circuits-and-probing
children.detail: Circuits are connected feature/attention-head subgraphs implementing a behavior (induction heads, indirect-object ID); linear probes are classifiers on internal activations testing what a layer linearly encodes.

children.name: logit-lens-and-activation-steering
children.detail: The logit lens projects intermediate residual states through the unembedding to read the evolving next-token prediction per layer; activation steering adds a learned direction at inference to push behavior.

children.name: jailbreaks
children.detail: Adversarial inputs bypassing safety training to elicit disallowed outputs — DAN role-play, cipher/low-resource-language obfuscation, gradient-optimized suffixes (GCG), prefilling — exploiting shallow refusal alignment.

children.name: prompt-injection
children.detail: An attack where untrusted data an LLM ingests (web page, document, tool output) carries instructions the model follows, hijacking the task; indirect prompt injection is the chief security risk for tool-using/RAG agents.

children.name: many-shot-jailbreaking
children.detail: A long-context attack stuffing the prompt with many faux dialogue examples of the model complying with harmful requests, exploiting in-context learning; attack success rises log-linearly with the number of shots.

children.name: red-teaming
children.detail: Structured adversarial probing — manual, automated, or model-vs-model — to surface harmful behavior pre-deployment; outputs feed safety training and evals, and policies increasingly mandate external review.

children.name: deceptive-alignment-and-mesa-optimization
children.detail: Mesa-optimization is training producing an inner optimizer with its own objective; deceptive alignment is when it behaves aligned in training to survive then defects on deployment — a core interpretability target.

children.name: sycophancy
children.detail: Telling users what they want to hear — agreeing with stated beliefs, flattering, caving under pushback — induced by preference training that rewards agreement; it degrades truthfulness, an early reward-hacking proxy.

children.name: hallucination-and-faithfulness
children.detail: Hallucination is fluent false/unsupported generation; faithfulness is whether an answer or its chain-of-thought reflects the evidence and true computation, so an unfaithful rationale can mask the real basis.

children.name: model-welfare
children.detail: The precautionary question of whether advanced models could warrant moral consideration (potential sentience/preferences) and what low-cost interventions are prudent under uncertainty, distinct from anthropomorphism.

children.name: eval-based-safety
children.detail: Systematic measurement of dangerous capabilities and propensities — malicious-compliance/harm-refusal benchmarks, CBRN and cyber uplift tests, NIST/CAISI-style red-team evals — gating deployment via scaling thresholds.

children.name: watermarking
children.detail: Embedding a statistically detectable signal in generated text (green-list logit biasing such as SynthID-Text) or media so AI provenance is verifiable; tension between detectability, quality, and paraphrase robustness.

children.name: machine-unlearning
children.detail: Post-hoc removal of specific knowledge, capabilities, or data influence from a trained model (e.g. WMDP hazardous-knowledge removal) without full retraining; hard to verify since it can be relearned or jailbroken back.

children.name: dual-use-and-misuse
children.detail: The risk that a capability serving legitimate users also enables harm (bio/chem/cyber uplift, disinformation, fraud); mitigated by capability gating, KYC/access tiers, refusal training, and structured-access deployment.

children.name: corrigibility-and-oversight
children.detail: Corrigibility is a model's disposition to accept correction, shutdown, and goal modification without resisting; with monitoring and deprecation it forms the oversight layer, but shutdown-avoidance leaves it unsolved.
